```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  lines <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  clean_lines <- sub("//.*$", "", lines)
  txt <- paste(clean_lines, collapse = "\n")
  txt <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", txt)
  fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("unified_silla_and_goryeo_korea.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("unified_silla_and_goryeo_korea_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("unified_silla_and_goryeo_korea_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  gyeonggi_gaegyeong = "Gyeonggi-Gaegyeong",
  yanggwang_chungcheong = "Yanggwang",
  jeolla_tamna = "Jeolla-Tamna",
  gyeongsang_silla = "Gyeongsang",
  gyoju_gangwon = "Gyoju",
  seohae_hwanghae = "Seohae",
  bukgye_pyongan = "Bukgye",
  donggye_hamgyong = "Donggye"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 424 urban, administrative, military and maritime settlements active across the Korean peninsula between 668AD and 1392AD, encompassing 226.901 km² across eight historical circuits. Synthesising dynastic chronicles (*Samguk Sagi*, *Samguk Yusa*, *Goryeosa*), the Shosoin village registers (*Silla Minjeongmunseo*), national heritage inventories, and classical cadastres [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Lee2016Bioanthropological; @KwonShin1977Joseon; @Cha2009LivingStandards], the register incorporates every primary administrative seat of the realm: the primary dynastic metropolises of Gyeongju (350k) and Kaesong (260k), secondary capitals including Pyongyang (150k), Seoul (99,5k), Buyeo (69,9k), Jeonju (30,3k), Gimhae (28,3k) and Gongju (25k), alongside regional military garrisons and coastal trading ports. Across the 424 catalogued settlements, the dataset documents 3.665 settlement-year population observations spanning 668AD to 1392AD (averaging 7,95 observations per centre). At the 1200AD mediaeval demographic peak, the leading urban centres were Kaesong (260k), Gyeongju (180k), Pyongyang (85k), Seoul (55,1k), Buyeo (35k), Jeonju (26k), Gimhae (24k), Daegu (16,8k) and Ulsan (15,2k). Alongside the 424 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 13 excluded candidate entries out of 437 total evaluated candidates.

# Background

Urbanisation in Unified Silla and Goryeo Korea was structured by the intersection of centralised dynastic administration, frontier military defence and maritime commercial networks [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Anon2010Buddhist; @Seungyeon2013Formation]. Under the administrative framework established by Unified Silla following the unification wars of 668AD, the peninsula was organized into Nine Provinces and Five Secondary Capitals (*Guju O-Sogyeong*), with the primary royal seat at Geumseong (Gyeongju) in the southeastern basin [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Lee2016Bioanthropological]. Geumseong accommodated a sophisticated gridded ward system, monumental Buddhist sanctuaries, and aristocratic estates supported by tax grain transport [@Barnes2015Archaeology].

Following the founding of Goryeo in 918AD and peninsular reunification in 936AD, political authority shifted to Gaegyeong (Kaesong), which developed into a cosmopolitan capital protected by inner and outer walls (*Manwoldae* and *Naseong*) [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Anon2010Buddhist]. Goryeo institutionalised a multi-capital system: Gaegyeong as the principal imperial seat, Seogyeong (Pyongyang) as the western bastion projecting military force into the northern frontier, Namgyeong (Seoul/Hanyang) as the southern capital, and Donggyeong (Gyeongju) preserving ancestral continuity in the southeast [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Lee2015Sketch].

Beyond the capitals, every civil county (*hyeon*) and military district (*jin*) possessed an administrative compound housing government magistrate offices, state granaries, confucian schools, and ancestral shrines [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Cha2009LivingStandards]. Along the northern border, fortified garrison citadels formed an integrated defensive shield along the Chongchon and Yalu river valleys, while maritime ports such as Byeongnando on the Yesong River and Cheonghaejin on Wando island handled overseas commerce with Song China, Liao, Jin and Japan [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Anon2010Buddhist].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by extracting historical administrative seats from dynastic chronicles and synchronising them with national heritage databases, archaeological excavation inventories and cadastral surveys [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Lee2016Bioanthropological; @KwonShin1977Joseon]. All 424 catalogued settlements carry verified historical coordinates and assign to one of the eight provincial circuit masks.

In the regional source ledger, 13 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair suburban entities within 8 km of canonical county seats, or locations situated outside mainland peninsular study bounds [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @KwonShin1977Joseon]. For example, duplicate records for Miryang, Wanju, Goseong and Daedeok were consolidated into their primary canonical seats, while Ulleung Island was classified as out of bounds for the contiguous peninsular mainland mask.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms 424 included settlements and 13 excluded candidate entries (437 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 424 settlements carry WGS84 geographic coordinates and non-zero population records for the historical benchmarks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the fifteen leading urban centres of the Korean peninsula.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-korea} presents the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the primacy of the dynastic capitals, regional secondary seats, and agricultural hubs across the Korean peninsula.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function (x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

get_pop_str <- function (e, y) {
  v <- e[["population"]][[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function (e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Province = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), "AD"),
    P750 = get_pop_str(e, "750"),
    P1200 = get_pop_str(e, "1200"),
    P1392 = get_pop_str(e, "1392"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in Korea ordered by peak documented population (n=424 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Province", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "750AD", "1200AD", "1392AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-korea", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-korea} summarises the distribution of settlements across all eight historical provincial territories alongside their leading urban centres. Bukgye leads all territories with 94 catalogued settlements, followed by Donggye (75), Gyeongsang (65), Seohae (50), Gyoju (47), Gyeonggi (46), Jeolla (45) and Yanggwang (39). Table \ref{tab:excluded-korea} details all 13 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function (e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement counts and leading urban centres across the eight Korean provincial territories (424 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-korea", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function (c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list, function (c) {
  just <- as.character(c[["justification"]])
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  just <- gsub("/", " or ", just, fixed = TRUE)
  just <- gsub("_", " ", just, fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = gsub("_", " ", c[["reason"]]),
    Consolidation_Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "All 13 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger, consolidated into canonical settlements or removed as out of bounds.",
  c("Candidate", "Territory", "Classification", "Consolidation Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-korea", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Discussion and Limitations

Two spatial factors affect urban population aggregation in this gazetteer. First, major historical metropolises such as Gyeongju and Kaesong incorporated dual administrative and palace enclosures: Gyeongju comprised the central royal palace (*Wolseong*), aristocratic mansions and major monastery compounds across the open basin, while Kaesong integrated both civil palace districts and merchant quarters along the Yesong River approach. These contiguous complexes are consolidated into unified metropolitan entities to avoid artificial fragmentation. Second, while primary administrative seats (*ju*, *bu*, *mok*, *gun*, *hyeon*) are thoroughly recorded, minor rural villages (*hyang*, *so*, *bugok*) and seasonal mountain fortress refuges (*sanseong*) lacking permanent civilian administration are represented through county-level rural densities rather than isolated urban points [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Biccone2017Medieval].
